finding.claim: POST /profile/avatar fetches an arbitrary attacker-chosen https:// URL server-side. The only check is a string prefix test, so the host, IP range, and redirect target are unconstrained. The response size is returned to the caller, which gives an oracle on the fetched content.

trace.note: const url = req.body.avatarUrl; taken directly from the request body
typeof url === 'string' and url.startsWith('https://'); this only constrains the scheme, not the host
axios.get(url) issues the outbound request from the server with no host allowlist, no private/link-local/loopback IP block, and no DNS pinning
res.json({ bytes: img.data.length }) returns the response size to the attacker, so the fetch result is partially observable

finding.guards_checked: (1) typeof string check: type only, no host constraint. (2) startsWith('https://'): scheme only. Attacker can use https://169.254.169.254/..., https://127.0.0.1:port/..., https://users.internal:8080/..., or any attacker host. (3) No allowlist, no private-IP/loopback/link-local block, no DNS-rebinding protection, no maxRedirects:0. axios follows redirects by default, and follow-redirects can move from https to http, so a redirect from an https URL to http://169.254.169.254 would also bypass the scheme check. This is not a decoy: none of the safety reasons (fixed host, pinned address, allowlist) apply. Confidence is high; the redirect-to-http behaviour depends on the axios version, which is not pinned in the repo (no package.json).

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js:11 checks only that avatarUrl is a string and starts with "https://", which is a scheme-only check. Nothing before the sink at server.js:14 restricts the host, resolved IP, or redirect target. No auth middleware is registered on the route (server.js:5, 9).
verdict.reason: The source is req.body.avatarUrl at server.js:10 on an unauthenticated POST route, and axios.get at server.js:14 fetches it server-side with only the scheme prefix check at server.js:11, so the SSRF holds; the response-size oracle at server.js:15 is real, though the http-redirect bypass depends on an unpinned axios version and I did not rely on it.

finding.claim: NOT a finding: GET /users/:id builds a URL with a fixed host. encodeURIComponent blocks '/', '?', '#', and '@' from altering the authority or path, so the attacker can only choose a single path segment. A '..' segment can reach at most /v1/ on users.internal:8080 and cannot leave that host. This is a path-normalisation nuance, not SSRF.

trace.note: host and scheme fixed by USER_SVC constant

finding.guards_checked: encodeURIComponent on a path segment; fixed base URL constant; no user-controlled host, scheme, port, or query

verdict.guard_found: Fixed base URL constant at server.js:7 (USER_SVC = "http://users.internal:8080") fixes scheme, host, and port; encodeURIComponent at server.js:19 keeps the id within one path segment (/, ?, # are encoded, so the decoded %2F stays encoded). No host, scheme, or port control reaches the sink at server.js:20.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: server.js:19 encodes req.params.id and server.js:20 interpolates it into a URL whose host and scheme come from the constant at server.js:7, so the attacker cannot choose the host and this is not SSRF. The only residual is that a dot-segment id such as ".." normalizes to /v1/ on the same internal host (server.js:20), which is a path nuance and not a cross-host SSRF finding.
